The heat exchanger geometry consists of a single tube with a length of 200mm and a shell diameter of 20mm.
The heat exchanger is modeled using a simplified geometry that accounts for planar symmetry and is cut in half vertically.
The k-omega turbulence model shows lower RMS residual levels, around 1e-06, indicating a tighter convergence compared to the k-epsilon model, which has residual levels around 1e-03.
The k-omega model shows a higher total heat transfer rate at the outlet of the inner tube compared to the k-epsilon model.
The study concludes that the k-omega model is best suited for the heat exchanger simulation, as it provides more accurate heat transfer predictions due to its tighter convergence.
Heat exchangers have a wide range of applications in industries such as food and beverages, petroleum, hydrocarbon processing, pharmaceutical, automotive, power, and marine.
The overall heat transfer coefficient is defined as the reciprocal of the sum of the individual heat transfer coefficients, the wall thickness, and the fouling resistance.
The two main heat transfer mechanisms discussed in the paper are conduction and convection, with radiation being less common in manufacturing industries.

The key equations used in the study are the energy balance equations (Equation 1 and Equation 2), the heat transfer equation (Equation 3), and the overall heat transfer coefficient equation (Equation 5).

The paper mentions that the specific heat of a fluid is the property that determines the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of the fluid by one degree Celsius.
The log mean temperature difference (LMTD) is used to estimate the average temperature difference across the heat exchanger, and a higher LMTD results in a smaller heat transfer area.
The heat transfer coefficient is defined as the heat transfer rate per unit area and unit temperature difference, and it is calculated separately for the external and internal fluids.
